honest.docker-cache-order: Docker caches each instruction as a layer. Because COPY . . comes first, changing any file, even one line of api/main.py, invalidates that layer and every layer after it, so pip install re-runs from scratch on every build and takes minutes. The requirements change far less often than the code, so if Docker saw requirements.txt on its own before the install step it could reuse the cached dependency layer.
honest.docker-weights: Baking them in makes the image huge, almost 2 GB, so every build, push and pull is slow for the whole pod. The upside is that the container is self-contained and starts straight away without downloading anything when it boots.
honest.docker-host-bind: Inside the container 127.0.0.1 is the container's own localhost, so uvicorn would only accept connections from inside the container. My browser's request comes from the host through the -p 8000 port mapping, which arrives on a different network interface, so nothing is listening there and I would get connection refused even though the logs say the server started.
honest.docker-root-user: Without a USER line the process runs as root inside the container, so an attacker who gets code execution through the upload bug could overwrite any file, read secrets from the environment or tamper with the model weights. Running as a non-root user limits the damage to what that one user can touch.
honest.docker-base-image: The full image is around a gigabyte because it ships compilers and system libraries, so it is slower to pull. Slim is much smaller and has fewer packages to patch, which shrinks the attack surface, but if a package needs gcc to build a wheel the install would fail on slim.
honest.torch-no-grad: Without no_grad, autograd records a computation graph for every operation so it could run backward later. That graph keeps the intermediate activations in memory, so over 2,000 images memory keeps growing and the laptop could run out of memory. The captions are the same because nothing ever uses the gradients; it only costs time and memory.
honest.torch-eval-once: model.eval() doesn't change the weights, it switches the model into inference mode and that state persists until someone calls model.train(). It changes how dropout and batch norm behave, so if it came after the first batch, that batch would run with dropout on and its captions would be random and inconsistent with the rest.
honest.torch-batch-size: With 64 the batch might not fit in memory on a laptop and the run could crash, and with 1 it is slower because there is more overhead per image when nothing runs in parallel.
